11461-armenian-literature-comprising-poe:
This revised 1904 edition of Armenian Literature, translated into English for the first time with an introduction by Robert Arnot, gathers poetry, drama, folk-lore, and classic traditions. Arnot explains that surviving ancient Armenian literature is meagre and largely ecclesiastical, because Christianity, preached by Thaddeus and Bartholomew and established under Gregory the Illuminator. led the Church to destroy pagan temples and seek to stamp out pagan poetry and heroic chants.

Folk memory preserved ballads the Church condemned, sung as late as the twelfth century, and fragments survive through that persistence. The collection's home-life portions, fasts, festivals, manners, and traditions, give its oriental color. For readers, it opens a literature long hidden behind ecclesiastical history.
25040-bilingualism-address-delivered-bef:
The Honorable N. A. Belcourt's address to the Quebec Canadian Club on Tuesday, March 28, 1916, takes up bilingualism and Ontario's school question. Asked to speak in English, Belcourt promises no speech but a simple, lucid explanation, addressed to intelligence rather than hearts, of a troublesome, distorted, and much misrepresented question. The trouble is not new in Ontario, he says, and has broken out again over the notorious Regulation No. 17, the center of the storm until its question is solved.

Belcourt pledges care, moderation, and concrete evidence for the regulation's real meaning, object, and effect, suppressing his own strong feelings for a calm and dispassionate analysis. He turns to Confederation's fathers, for whom both languages in the Federal Parliament and courts stood beyond doubt. He asks why English was safeguarded in Quebec's legislature while French was not named for Ontario's. The address is advocacy in measured tones.
armenian-literature-comprising-poetry-dr: Robert Arnot presents Armenian poetry, drama, folk lore, and classic tradition in English translation for the first time in this form. He notes that early pagan songs were largely lost when Gregory the Illuminator spread the Christian faith and stamped out temple verse. Much that survives is church writing, yet home life, fasts, festivals, and manners still shine through. The volume opens a rich national literature to readers who knew it only by name.
doe-osti-17198161-population-balance-equ:
Matthew Christian and David Luxat of Sandia lay out population balance equations for particles moving in liquids, in report SAND2026-27273 printed September 2026. A population balance tracks how many particles of each size exist as they form, grow, clump, break, dissolve, and settle. The opening chapter ties the method to molten salt reactors, where such particles affect operation.

Middle chapters build the continuous equation and its distribution function. A prescriptive numerical form follows for a coupled system: suspended particles, dissolved species, and deposits on surfaces, all moving through a network of control volumes. Terms for aggregation, breakup, nucleation, growth, dissolution, deposition, and resuspension are written out one by one. Discussion closes with the experiments still needed to validate the models.
doe-osti-2589612-i-v-curve-analysis-of-s:
A Sandia National Laboratories paper by Aaron Coll, Francis Alcorn, and Alec Talin, dated 15 September 2025, probes single particles of a candidate solar fuel material. The material is strontium titanate doped with aluminum, a semiconductor that may split water with sunlight. Its charge behavior is still poorly understood, so the team measured one particle at a time.

Particles sat on a gold base inside an electron microscope, touched by a gold probe. Current and voltage curves were taken in the dark and under the electron beam, sweeping the full range four times per particle. Fits gave a doping density near ten to the 22.1 per cubic centimeter, within about one order of magnitude, and a built-in voltage of about 0.84 volts, give or take 0.45. Diffusion times came from the same curves.
doe-osti-3374633-introductory-review-of-:
INL/RPT-23-75822, an Idaho National Laboratory report, Revision 2, dated September 2025, by Sanjay Haresh Mukhi, surveys the rules that would govern nuclear power at sea. It is an entry-level review from the Maritime Nuclear Applications Group. The report maps which agencies and treaties touch a reactor on a ship or a floating plant. It also covers new IAEA terms and proposed definitions for this young field.

One theme is that most rulebooks grew up around one home-grown reactor type. Canada shaped its rules around heavy water reactors. Russia built its framework around sodium and lead fast reactors. The report praises Canada and the United Kingdom for a shift toward performance-based rules. Under that style, a new design can win approval by proving equal or better results with sound evidence.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AssassinationJF: Canada's Maclean's magazine marked the thirtieth anniversary of the Kennedy assassination in 1993 with coverage looking back at Dallas, and this file holds that material as captured in the archive. Anniversary issues took stock of the case at each decade mark. They weighed what was known, what was still fought over, and how the event lived in public memory. The Maclean's coverage gives the view from outside the United States, from a country that watched the story as a close neighbor.
